name: Version Control Operations Using Git
problemStatement: Create a Git repository for a project named Student Management System and perform basic version control operations.
tasks: Initialize a local Git repository.
Create a file named student.txt and add sample student information.
Stage and commit the file with the message "Initial commit".
Create a remote repository on GitHub and link it with the local repository.
Push the commit to the remote repository.
Create a new branch named feature-update.
Modify the student.txt file by adding additional student records.
Commit the changes in the feature-update branch.
Merge feature-update into the main branch.
Display the commit history using Git commands.
Write a brief conclusion.

steps.title: Initialize a Local Git Repository
steps.description: Create a project directory named StudentManagementSystem and initialize a new local Git repository.
steps.commands:
mkdir StudentManagementSystem
cd StudentManagementSystem
git init
steps.output: Initialized empty Git repository in C:/.../StudentManagementSystem/.git/

steps.title: Create student.txt with Sample Student Records
steps.description: Create a new text file named student.txt in the root of the repository and add sample student information.
steps.commandTip:
On Windows PowerShell, run: Set-Content -Path student.txt -Value @'
(paste content above)
'@

steps.title: Stage and Commit with Message "Initial commit"
steps.description: Add student.txt to the Git staging index and create the first commit.
steps.commands:
git add student.txt
git commit -m "Initial commit"
steps.output:
[main (root-commit) 3f2b1a0] Initial commit
 1 file changed, 8 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 student.txt

steps.title: Link Local Repository with Remote GitHub Repository
steps.description: Create an empty repository named StudentManagementSystem on GitHub, then add it as remote origin.
steps.commands:
# Replace <your-username> with your actual GitHub username:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/StudentManagementSystem.git
git branch -M main
git remote -v

steps.title: Push the Commit to Remote GitHub Repository
steps.description: Push the main branch commit to the remote GitHub repository.
steps.output:
Enumerating objects: 3, done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 280 bytes | 280.00 KiB/s, done.
To https://github.com/<your-username>/StudentManagementSystem.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

steps.title: Create and Switch to Branch feature-update
steps.description: Create an isolated feature branch named feature-update to work on new records without affecting main.

steps.title: Modify student.txt by Adding Additional Student Records
steps.description: Append additional student records (Roll 104 and 105) to student.txt.
steps.commandTip: Review diff before staging: git diff student.txt

steps.title: Commit Changes in the feature-update Branch
steps.description: Stage the modified student.txt and commit changes in the feature-update branch.
steps.commands:
git add student.txt
git commit -m "Add student records for roll 104 and 105"
git push -u origin feature-update
steps.output:
[feature-update 7a9c3d1] Add student records for roll 104 and 105
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)

steps.title: Merge feature-update Branch into main Branch
steps.description: Switch back to the main branch and merge the feature-update branch changes.
steps.commands:
git checkout main
git merge feature-update
git push origin main
steps.output:
Updating 3f2b1a0..7a9c3d1
Fast-forward
 student.txt | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)

steps.title: Display Commit History Using Git Commands
steps.description: View the graphical and formatted one-line commit log.
steps.output:
* 7a9c3d1 (HEAD -> main, origin/main, feature-update) Add student records for roll 104 and 105
* 3f2b1a0 (origin/main) Initial commit

conclusion: In this experiment, essential version control operations using Git were executed for the Student Management System. We initialized a local Git repository, created and committed tracked student records, established connection with a remote GitHub repository, and pushed the commit history. Furthermore, non-linear branch management was demonstrated by isolating work inside the feature-update branch, followed by a fast-forward merge into the main branch. The graphical commit log confirmed complete traceability of changes.
fullScript:
# ========================================================
# EXPERIMENT 1: Version Control Operations Using Git
# Project: Student Management System
# ========================================================

# 1. Initialize local repository
mkdir StudentManagementSystem
cd StudentManagementSystem
git init

# 2. Create student.txt with sample records
cat << 'EOF' > student.txt
=========================================
       STUDENT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM         
=========================================
Roll No | Name           | Branch | Year
--------|----------------|--------|-----
101     | Alice Johnson  | CSE    | 3rd 
102     | Bob Smith      | CSE    | 3rd 
103     | Charlie Brown  | IT     | 3rd 
=========================================
EOF

# 3. Stage and commit with message 'Initial commit'
git add student.txt
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# 4. Link remote GitHub repository and push main branch
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/StudentManagementSystem.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

# 5. Create new branch 'feature-update'
git checkout -b feature-update

# 6. Add additional student records to student.txt
cat << 'EOF' >> student.txt
104     | Diana Prince   | AIML   | 3rd 
105     | Evan Wright    | CSE    | 3rd 
=========================================
EOF

# 7. Commit changes in feature-update
git add student.txt
git commit -m "Add student records for roll 104 and 105"
git push -u origin feature-update

# 8. Merge feature-update into main
git checkout main
git merge feature-update
git push origin main

# 9. Display commit history
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

# Conclusion:
# Version control operations using Git were successfully performed for the Student Management System.
# We initialized a local repository, tracked and committed files, linked to remote GitHub, managed
# branches cleanly, and verified commit history with git log.
note: Make sure you create an empty repository named 'StudentManagementSystem' on GitHub before executing the push command.

name: Implementation of CI/CD Pipelines Using GitHub Actions and Jenkins
problemStatement: Create a simple Node.js project and implement Continuous Integration (CI) using GitHub Actions and a Jenkins Pipeline to automate build and test processes.
tasks: Create a Node.js project with a test script using Jest.
Create a GitHub repository and push the project files.
Create a workflow file ci.yml inside .github/workflows/.
Configure GitHub Actions workflow to: Checkout source code, Setup Node.js, Install dependencies, Run test cases.
Install and configure Jenkins.
Create a Jenkins Pipeline job.
Add a Jenkinsfile with the stages: Checkout, Install, Test, Build.
Execute both pipelines and verify successful execution.
Capture screenshots of GitHub Actions workflow run & Jenkins Pipeline Console Output.
Compare GitHub Actions and Jenkins based on setup and execution.
Write a brief conclusion.

steps.title: Create Node.js Project Structure
steps.description: Initialize a new Node.js project directory and install Jest as a development testing dependency.
steps.commands:
mkdir cicd-demo-app
cd cicd-demo-app
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev jest

steps.title: Configure package.json with Test & Build Scripts
steps.description: Update package.json to define test (Jest) and build scripts.

file.name: package.json

steps.title: Create Application Code (src/app.js)
steps.description: Create src/app.js with basic mathematical operations to be tested.

file.name: src/app.js

steps.title: Create Jest Test Script (tests/app.test.js)
steps.description: Create tests/app.test.js with test suites verifying add and multiply functions.

file.name: tests/app.test.js

steps.title: Create GitHub Actions Workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
steps.description: Create .github/workflows/ci.yml to trigger automated tests and build on push/pull-request.

file.name: .github/workflows/ci.yml
file.content:
name: Node.js CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ "main" ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ "main" ]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # 1. Checkout source code
      - name: Checkout Source Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # 2. Setup Node.js
      - name: Setup Node.js 20
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: 'npm'

      # 3. Install dependencies
      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm install

      # 4. Run test cases
      - name: Run Jest Test Cases
        run: npm test

      # 5. Build project
      - name: Run Build Step
        run: npm run build

steps.title: Push Project to GitHub
steps.description: Commit files and push to GitHub so the GitHub Actions workflow triggers automatically.
steps.commands:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Add Node.js project and GitHub Actions CI workflow"
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/cicd-demo-app.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

    ✓ correctly multiplies two numbers: 4 * 6 = 24 (1 ms)

steps.title: Comparison: GitHub Actions vs Jenkins
steps.description: Comparative analysis based on setup, maintenance, and execution.

comparison.gha: Git Push, PR, Issues, Webhooks, Schedules

comparison.jenkins: Admin manages server OS, security & plugins

comparison.gha: Generous free tier included with GitHub

conclusion: Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines were successfully implemented using both GitHub Actions and Jenkins for an automated Node.js application. Jest unit test cases and build processes were triggered automatically on each commit. GitHub Actions offered effortless cloud configuration with zero maintenance overhead, while Jenkins demonstrated high flexibility, granular plugin support, and robust control suitable for private enterprise infrastructure.

name: Create and Manage a Scrum-Based Agile Project in Jira
problemStatement: A software development team is developing an Online Library Management System. Using Jira, create a new Scrum project, configure workflow columns, create work items, organize the backlog, run a sprint, and demonstrate team collaboration.
tasks: Create a new Scrum project/space.
Configure the workflow columns as: To Do, In Progress, In Review, Done.
Create at least four work items: Two Tasks, One Story, One Bug.
Assign priorities and descriptions to each work item.
Organize the work items in the backlog.
Create a sprint and add all work items to the sprint.
Move at least one item through all workflow stages up to "Done".
Invite a team member (or demonstrate the invite feature).
Write a brief conclusion on the benefits of Agile project management using Jira.

steps.title: Create a New Scrum Project in Jira
steps.description: Log into Atlassian Jira and initialize a new Scrum project for the Online Library Management System.
guiSteps: Open your Jira instance (https://<your-domain>.atlassian.net).
Click on Projects in the top navigation bar -> select Create Project.
Select Project Template: Scrum (Software Development).
Choose Project Type: Team-managed or Company-managed.
Enter Project Name: Online Library Management System
Enter Project Key: OLMS
Click Create Project.

steps.title: Configure the 4 Workflow Board Columns
steps.description: Customize the active Scrum board columns to reflect the required delivery stages.
guiSteps: Go to your project Board view.
Click the '...' menu at the top right -> select Board settings (or click '+ Add column').
Configure the 4 workflow columns with their mapped statuses:
1. [To Do]        -> Category: To Do
2. [In Progress]  -> Category: In Progress
3. [In Review]    -> Category: In Progress (Quality Gate)
4. [Done]         -> Category: Done
Save changes to ensure each column correctly transitions issues.

steps.title: Create Four Work Items (2 Tasks, 1 Story, 1 Bug)
steps.description: Create the 4 required work items with priorities, descriptions, and story points.

items.summary: User Search and Browse Book Catalog
items.description:
As a registered student,
I want to search books by Title, Author, or ISBN,
So that I can check real-time shelf availability and location before visiting the library.
items.acceptance:
1. Search results return in < 1 second.
2. Shows status (Available / Borrowed).

items.summary: Design PostgreSQL Database Schema for Books and Borrowing Records
items.description: Design relational schema including tables for books, authors, members, and transactions with foreign key constraints and ISBN indexing.

items.summary: Configure JWT User Authentication and Role-Based Access Control
items.description: Implement authentication endpoints with password hashing (bcrypt) and role guards for Student and Librarian access.

items.summary: Duplicate Borrow Record Created on Rapid Double-Click of 'Confirm Borrow'
items.description:
When a student double-clicks the confirm button quickly, two identical database rows are inserted with duplicate transaction IDs.
Fix by disabling the submit button on initial click and adding a database uniqueness constraint.

steps.title: Organize Work Items in the Backlog
steps.description: Rank and prioritize work items in the Product Backlog.
guiSteps: Open the Backlog view from the left project sidebar.
Drag and drop work items to prioritize them in the backlog stack:
1. OLMS-4 (Critical Bug: Duplicate borrow error) - Ranked Highest
2. OLMS-2 (Task: DB schema design) - Ranked High
3. OLMS-1 (Story: Book Search & Catalog) - Ranked High
4. OLMS-3 (Task: JWT Authentication & RBAC) - Ranked Medium

steps.title: Create Sprint and Add All Work Items
steps.description: Create Sprint 1, assign all work items into it, and start the sprint.
guiSteps: In the Backlog view, click Create Sprint (creates 'OLMS Sprint 1').
Drag all 4 work items from the Backlog section into 'OLMS Sprint 1'.
Click Start Sprint on the sprint header.
Fill in sprint configuration details:
- Sprint Name: OLMS Sprint 1 - Core Catalog & Auth
- Duration: 2 weeks
- Sprint Goal: Deliver functional book catalog search and resolve transaction race conditions.
Click Start to launch the active sprint board.

steps.title: Move Work Items Through Workflow Stages to 'Done'
steps.description: Simulate real-time task progression across the Kanban/Scrum board.
guiSteps: Go to the active Sprint Board.
Drag Story OLMS-1 from [To Do] -> [In Progress] (Development begins).
Drag Story OLMS-1 from [In Progress] -> [In Review] (Code review & PR submitted).
Drag Story OLMS-1 from [In Review] -> [Done] (PR merged, QA passed, acceptance criteria met).
Observe Jira automatically updating completion stats and burn-down chart progress.

steps.title: Demonstrate Inviting a Team Member
steps.description: Invite developers or collaborators to the Jira project space.
guiSteps: Click Project Settings (gear icon in left sidebar) -> select Access or People.
Click Add people (top-right).
Enter teammate email: teammate@university.edu
Select Role: Developer or Member.
Click Add (demonstrating team invitation & role-based permissions).

conclusion: Agile project management was successfully demonstrated using Jira for the Online Library Management System. We configured a Scrum project, set up a customized 4-stage workflow (To Do, In Progress, In Review, Done), created categorized user stories, tasks, and bugs with story points and priorities, and planned a time-boxed sprint. Moving items across the board demonstrated work-in-progress visibility, while Jira's automated sprint tracking and collaboration features demonstrated modern agile team governance.
fullScript:
# Jira Agile Scrum Setup Guide for Online Library Management System (OLMS)
# 1. Project Template: Scrum | Name: Online Library Management System | Key: OLMS
# 2. Workflow Columns: To Do, In Progress, In Review, Done
# 3. Work Items Created:
#    - Story (OLMS-1): User Search and Browse Book Catalog (5 pts, High)
#    - Task (OLMS-2): Design PostgreSQL Database Schema (High)
#    - Task (OLMS-3): Configure JWT Authentication & RBAC (Medium)
#    - Bug (OLMS-4): Duplicate borrow record on rapid click (Critical)
# 4. Sprint: OLMS Sprint 1 (2 weeks)
# 5. Demonstrated transitions: To Do -> In Progress -> In Review -> Done
# 6. Team member invite demonstrated via Project Settings -> Access.
note: Remember the key Scrum artifacts for viva: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment, and the Sprint Burn-down Chart.

name: Containerizing Applications Using Docker
problemStatement: Create a Docker container for a simple Java application and demonstrate the process of building a Docker image and running the application inside a container. The experiment should include Docker installation, Dockerfile creation, image building, container execution, and verification of application output.
tasks: Install Docker Desktop on the system.
Create a folder named DockerDemo.
Write a simple Java program that displays: Hello Docker World.
Create a Dockerfile without any extension.
Navigate to the project directory using PowerShell.
Build the Docker image using: docker build -t dockerdemo .
Verify that the image is created successfully: docker images.
Run the container: docker run dockerdemo.
Open Docker Desktop and inspect created container for logs & execution details.
Record the output and container status.
Write a brief conclusion.

steps.title: Install and Verify Docker Desktop
steps.description: Download and install Docker Desktop with WSL 2 backend. Verify the Docker CLI is accessible.

steps.title: Create Project Directory DockerDemo
steps.description: Create a dedicated folder named DockerDemo and navigate into it using PowerShell.

steps.title: Write Java Application (HelloDocker.java)
steps.description: Create HelloDocker.java that prints 'Hello Docker World'.

file.name: HelloDocker.java

steps.title: Create the Dockerfile (No Extension)
steps.description: Create a file named 'Dockerfile' without any extension in the DockerDemo directory.

file.name: Dockerfile
file.content:
# Step 1: Use official lightweight OpenJDK base image
FROM openjdk:17-jdk-alpine

# Step 2: Set working directory inside container
WORKDIR /app

# Step 3: Copy Java source code into container
COPY HelloDocker.java .

# Step 4: Compile the Java program
RUN javac HelloDocker.java

# Step 5: Specify entrypoint command to run on startup
CMD ["java", "HelloDocker"]

steps.commandTip: Make sure the file name is strictly 'Dockerfile' (not Dockerfile.txt).

steps.title: Navigate to Project Directory in PowerShell
steps.description: Ensure your PowerShell session is positioned inside the DockerDemo directory containing both files.

conclusion: In this experiment, a Java application was successfully containerized using Docker. We authored a multi-instruction Dockerfile, compiled the HelloDocker.java source code inside an isolated Alpine Linux environment, and packaged it into a self-contained image tagged 'dockerdemo'. Running the container produced the exact expected output 'Hello Docker World' with an exit code of 0. This demonstrates container immutability, zero-dependency hosting, and elimination of environment inconsistency.
